Emergency Medicaid
•Even though undocumented immigrants are not eligible for full Medicaid coverage, they can receive Emergency Medicaid for life-threatening conditions, childbirth, and other emergency care.
•Hospitals submit claims to the state Medicaid program, which then reimburses for emergency services only—not for routine or follow-up care.
•This is one of the main formal reimbursement channels.

Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) Payments
•Hospitals that treat a high percentage of uninsured and low-income patients (including undocumented patients) receive federal DSH funds through Medicaid.
•These payments are meant to offset the costs of uncompensated care but don’t fully cover them.

State and Local Programs
•Some states (e.g., California, New York, Illinois) have programs that expand coverage or reimburse hospitals for care provided to undocumented residents, including preventive or specialty care in addition to emergencies.
•Funding comes from state budgets, county health systems, or special immigrant health funds.

Federal Reimbursement Programs
•Congress has occasionally authorized special funds (like Section 1011 of the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003) to reimburse hospitals for emergency care provided to undocumented immigrants.
•These programs are temporary, capped, and relatively limited in scope compared to total costs

Cost Shifting and Charity Care
•When reimbursement doesn’t cover costs, hospitals absorb the losses as charity care or bad debt.
•To compensate, hospitals often shift costs indirectly to insured patients through higher charges, or rely on philanthropic contributions and hospital operating budgets.
